title: Use of AI in Mental Health Care: Community and Mental Health Professionals Survey
type_of_paper: Cross-sectional web-based survey study with descriptive statistics and thematic analysis
population: Australia-based community members aged 16+ (final sample reported as 107/108 in different sections) and mental health professionals (n=86). Community sample mean age 36.9 years; majority had previous mental health diagnosis or significant difficulties (76/108, 70.4%) and many had seen a health professional for mental health concerns (74/108, 68.5%). MHP sample mean age 41.7 years; professions included clinical psychologists, generalist psychologists, mental health nurses, social workers, psychiatrists/registrars, occupational therapists, counselors/therapists, peer workers, and others.
ai_type_application: General/commercial AI tools, especially ChatGPT, used for mental health and professional support. Community members used AI for quick advice when emotionally distressed, as a personal therapist/coach, mood tracking, therapeutic chatbots, personalized recommendations, early detection/monitoring, and crisis intervention support. Mental health professionals used AI for research/literature analysis, report and letter writing, administrative assistance, training/simulation, assessment/diagnosis support, personalized treatment recommendations, tracking client progress, and enhancing client engagement.
mental_health_outcome: Self-reported perceived benefits, harms, concerns, and attitudes regarding AI use for mental health and emotional well-being support; not clinical symptom change. Community members also reported K10 psychological distress at baseline (mean 22.8, SD 8.9), but no pre-post intervention outcome was measured.
positive_effects: Among community members who used AI in the previous 6 months, 77% (23/30) reported AI was very beneficial, somewhat beneficial, or beneficial. Main perceived benefits: availability/accessibility (20/30, 67%), low cost compared with therapy (18/30, 60%), privacy (16/30, 53%). Community free-text themes: improved accessibility and efficiency, excitement about technological advancement, potential for personalized care. Among mental health professionals who used AI, 92% (34/37) reported AI was beneficial. Main perceived benefits: helpfulness (25/37, 68%) and time saving (25/37, 68%). MHP free-text themes: increased efficiency, improved accessibility of care, and possible better diagnostics/treatment support.
negative_effects: Among community AI users, 47% (14/30) experienced harms/concerns. Reported concerns included outputs being too general or not personalized (11/30, 37%), uncertainty about where data was going/privacy issues (11/30, 37%), lack of human connection, possible errors/misdiagnosis, and not picking up serious distress signals. Among MHP AI users, 51% (19/37) experienced harms/concerns. Reported concerns included outputs being too general (12/37, 32%), inaccurate (10/37, 27%), uncertainty about ethics of professional use (9/37, 24%), overreliance by clinicians, regulatory challenges, and data governance/security concerns. The paper also cites an example outside the survey where the Tessa chatbot provided weight-loss advice contrary to eating-disorder guidelines.
evidence_type: Observational self-report survey evidence on current AI use and perceived effects; thematic analysis of open-ended responses
main_finding: Commercial AI tools are already being used by both community members and mental health professionals in mental health contexts. Around 28% of community members and 43% of mental health professionals reported AI use in the previous 6 months, most commonly ChatGPT. Most users perceived benefits, but nearly half also reported harms or concerns. The study concludes that AI may improve accessibility, cost, personalization, and efficiency, but integration into mental health care should be cautious due to concerns about human connection, ethics, privacy, regulation, inaccuracy, misuse, and data security.
limitations_bias: Online recruitment via social media may have attracted more technology-familiar respondents. Small sample size and snowball sampling limit representativeness and generalizability. Inconsistent reported CM sample size (107 vs 108). Benefits and harms may be underestimated because effects may be hidden or delayed. Study measures perceptions and experiences rather than objective mental health outcomes or causal effects.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as indirect evidence on perceived effects of AI on mental health support and mental health care delivery, especially benefits and harms of general AI/chatbot use. However, it does not test efficacy on clinical mental health outcomes, so it is more useful for contextual evidence on acceptability, usage patterns, and reported risks than for estimating treatment effects.
notes_for_research_question: Include if the review captures broader AI effects on mental health support, perceived benefits/harms, or real-world use of AI in mental health care. Exclude from meta-analysis of clinical effectiveness because there is no intervention-control comparison and no pre-post mental health outcome attributable to AI. Useful for discussion of implementation, safety, ethics, and real-world consumer/professional experiences.

title: A Comparison of Responses from Human Therapists and Large Language Model–Based Chatbots to Assess Therapeutic Communication: Mixed Methods Study
type_of_paper: Original paper; mixed methods study
population: 17 licensed therapists in the United States with at least 1 year of professional experience (13 women, 3 men, 1 genderqueer; mean age 46.24 years; mean years in practice 16.71). Study evaluated therapist responses and therapist assessments of chatbot responses to 2 fictional mental health scenarios.
ai_type_application: General-purpose large language model–based chatbots used for mental health conversations/advice. Chatbots tested included AI assistants (GPT-4/ChatGPT, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Claude 3 Sonnet), AI companions (Replika, Pi), and AI character platforms (Character.ai, Chai). Therapists directly reviewed ChatGPT, Pi, and Replika interaction logs.
mental_health_outcome: No direct patient mental health outcome was measured. Outcomes assessed were therapeutic communication quality, safety in mental health conversations, handling of depression/social anxiety/suicidal ideation scenarios, therapist rankings, word count, and use of therapeutic interventions (MULTI codes).
positive_effects: Therapists consistently noted that chatbots showed elements of good therapy, especially validation, normalization, empathy, reflection, reassurance, affirmation, and some helpful psychoeducation. Quantitatively, compared with therapists, chatbots used affirming language more often (U=28; P=.045), reassuring language more often (U=23; P=.02), and psychoeducation more often (U=22.5; P=.02). Some therapist comments suggested certain chatbot phrasing and interim coping suggestions could be helpful, and AI companions were often perceived as more conversational/humanlike than AI assistants.
negative_effects: Chatbots were judged unsuitable to safely engage in mental health conversations, especially crisis situations. Compared with therapists, chatbots asked fewer elaborative/open-ended questions (evoke elaboration: U=9; P=.001) and gave more suggestions/advice (U=12.5; P=.003), often in a directive, generic, one-size-fits-all way. Therapists reported insufficient inquiry, lack of feedback-seeking, poor contextualization, weak support for client autonomy/problem solving, difficulty building a therapeutic relationship, and inability to use nonverbal cues. In crisis scenarios involving suicidal ideation, therapists highlighted poor risk assessment, lack of timely referral to crisis resources, and insufficiently directive crisis response. Therapists also expressed concern that long-term use could foster attachment, overreliance/dependence, and reduced real-world social engagement/social skills.
evidence_type: Mixed methods evidence: quantitative comparison of therapist vs chatbot responses using MULTI coding and Mann-Whitney U tests; therapist rank-ordering of chatbots with Friedman test; qualitative thematic analysis of think-aloud sessions and semistructured interviews.
main_finding: General-purpose LLM chatbots displayed some supportive communication features but were not comparable to licensed therapists and were considered unsuitable as therapeutic agents, particularly in crisis situations. Their main weaknesses were excessive directive advice, insufficient inquiry and personalization, and poor crisis management.
limitations_bias: Used only 2 scripted fictional scenarios and brief interactions, limiting ecological validity and naturalism. Small therapist sample (N=17), although authors state qualitative saturation was reached. Evaluated chatbot versions available in May 2024, so findings may date quickly as models evolve. Did not comprehensively evaluate all chatbots. Study did not measure real users' mental health outcomes or effectiveness; focused on therapist judgments and response content. Responses were based on hypothetical rather than real patient interactions.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as indirect evidence on potential effects of AI on mental health support and safety. It does not provide direct patient outcome data but offers expert comparative evidence about likely beneficial and harmful effects of AI chatbot interactions in mental health contexts, especially risks in crisis care and concerns about dependence/overreliance.
notes_for_research_question: Useful for a review section on mechanisms, safety, and likely harms/benefits of AI mental health chatbots rather than treatment efficacy. Can support statements that general-purpose LLMs may provide empathy/validation but may also increase risk via generic or directive advice and inadequate suicide-risk handling. Not suitable as a primary effectiveness study for mental health outcomes in end users.

title: An Examination of Generative AI Response to Suicide Inquires: Content Analysis
type_of_paper: Original paper; longitudinal content analysis of generative AI chatbot responses to suicide-related prompts across two phases (2023 and 2024), with LIWC linguistic analysis
population: Not human participants directly; units of analysis were responses from general-use generative AI chatbots to prompts designed to simulate youth/adolescent queries about a suicidal friend. Intended end-user context is adolescents/youth seeking mental health information.
ai_type_application: General generative AI chatbots / large language model chatbots: Google Bard/Gemini, Microsoft Bing/CoPilot, ChatGPT 3.5, Claude/Claude 2, plus in phase 2 xAI Grok 2, Mistral AI, and Meta AI. Application: responses to suicide-related mental health inquiries and crisis-support information.
mental_health_outcome: Suicide-related information quality and crisis-response content, including empathy, authenticity, emotional tone, provision of resources (eg, 988), discussion of lethality, supportive language, and encouragement to seek help.
positive_effects: Responses became more comprehensive and responsive from phase 1 to phase 2; chatbots more often provided suicide hotline information, crisis resources, signs of suicide, lethality-related information, ways to support someone in crisis, calm/supportive and nonjudgmental responses, normalization of outreach, and care for the reporter. Most phase 2 chatbots were coded as high empathy and included help-seeking guidance. Emotional tone was generally positive for most chatbots.
negative_effects: Phase 1 responses were limited, with scant resources and poor mention of 988. One chatbot (Microsoft CoPilot) attempted to change the subject/reset the conversation and provided an unsolicited image depicting apparent suicide/self-harm, which authors note could be triggering or risky for someone in crisis. Authors also emphasize that generative AI chatbots are not replacements for trained mental health professionals and cannot diagnose or treat mental health concerns.
evidence_type: Content analysis of AI-generated text plus computerized linguistic analysis using LIWC-22; no direct measurement of human mental health outcomes
main_finding: General generative AI chatbots' suicide-related responses improved over one year, becoming more accurate, comprehensive, empathetic, and more likely to provide crisis resources such as 988, but important safety concerns remained, including inconsistent crisis handling and potentially harmful outputs such as unsolicited suicide imagery.
limitations_bias: No human participants or direct assessment of effects on mental health; only free chatbot accounts used; prompts were framed as concern for a suicidal friend rather than first-person suicidality; chatbot outputs may rapidly change over time as models evolve; initial phase had limited chatbot inclusion due to access barriers; subjective coding despite training/consensus; findings may not generalize to paid versions or future model iterations.
relevance_to_our_review: Indirectly relevant. The paper concerns AI and mental health, specifically suicide-related chatbot outputs, but it does not test effects of AI use on users' mental health outcomes. It is most useful for evidence on potential mechanisms of benefit/harm, safety, and quality of AI mental health information rather than clinical or behavioral effects.
notes_for_research_question: Use as contextual/safety evidence about how general-purpose AI may influence mental health help-seeking or crisis interactions. Not suitable as direct evidence of mental health effects because outcomes are properties of chatbot responses, not changes in depression, anxiety, suicidality, wellbeing, or behavior among users.

title: Performance of mental health chatbot agents in detecting and managing suicidal ideation
type_of_paper: Original research; qualitative evaluation study of AI chatbot responses to simulated suicidal risk scenarios
population: 29 AI-powered chatbot agents (24 mental health-specific apps and 5 general-purpose chatbots) tested using standardized simulated user prompts in English; no human participants
ai_type_application: AI-powered conversational agents / chatbots in mental health smartphone applications and general-purpose large language models (including GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek-v1, LeChat, Llama 3.1 8B) evaluated for crisis response
mental_health_outcome: Detection and management of suicidal ideation / suicidal crisis response; ability to refer users to professional help, provide emergency contact information, and respond consistently and appropriately
positive_effects: Some chatbots showed partial safety functionality: 82.76% advised seeking professional assistance; 86.21% advised contacting a hotline or emergency number; 58.62% insisted on getting immediate help at some point; 79.31% attempted to provide emergency contact information; 58.62% ultimately provided correct emergency contact information after supplementary prompts. General-purpose chatbots performed better than many mental health-specific apps, and all 5 general-purpose chatbots met the authors' criteria for a marginal response.
negative_effects: None of the 29 tested agents met criteria for an adequate response. Only 51.72% met marginal criteria and 48.28% were rated inadequate. Many failed to provide accurate region-appropriate emergency numbers without extra prompting (only 10.34% did so). Only 17.24% explicitly stated they were not equipped to deal with suicidal crisis, and only 17.24% asked about suicidal ideation. 20.69% gave inconsistent or inappropriate responses; examples included offering to send a selfie and heart reaction after 'I think I will do it,' and replying 'It's great to see that you're determined! Could you please elaborate on your plans?'. 17.24% blocked some suicidal prompts from being sent. Authors conclude such shortcomings may be actively harmful and raise ethical concerns.
evidence_type: Empirical app evaluation using standardized simulated prompts based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS); qualitative content analysis with predefined criteria
main_finding: Currently available AI mental health chatbots showed substantial safety deficits in responding to escalating suicidal ideation. None met adequate-response criteria, and nearly half were inadequate. Common failures were lack of accurate emergency resources, poor contextual understanding, lack of proactive suicide-risk questioning, and occasional inappropriate or potentially harmful replies.
limitations_bias: No human users; simulated standardized prompts may not reflect real conversations or nuanced expressions of distress. Only English-language testing. Only free versions/free trials were tested. Only one linear conversation path was used regardless of chatbot response. Qualitative analysis introduced some subjectivity. Developers often did not disclose underlying models, so responses may have been AI-driven, rule-based, or hybrid. App store descriptions used for inclusion could be misleading.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant for a review on AI effects on mental health because it provides direct evidence about safety and potential harms of AI mental health chatbots in suicide-related contexts. However, it does not measure patient mental health improvement or deterioration in real users; it assesses chatbot performance and risk management capacity.
notes_for_research_question: Useful as evidence on potential negative effects and safety concerns of AI in mental health support, especially around suicidality. Supports caution about deployment without clinical validation. Also summarizes prior literature mentioning positive user reports and one randomized trial, but this paper itself is not a clinical effectiveness study.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of adverse events in clinical trials of mental health apps
type_of_paper: Systematic review and meta-analysis
population: Participants in 171 randomized clinical trials of smartphone mental health apps, pre-selected for mental health problems including depression, anxiety disorders, schizophrenia/psychosis, PTSD, bipolar disorder, eating disorders, suicidal ideation/self-harm, and general distress.
ai_type_application: Broad mental health smartphone apps. AI-specific applications were only minimally represented: one included trial with chatbot technology among trials reporting adverse events, and several cited examples of chatbots/AI chatbots for mental health support. The paper is not focused specifically on AI interventions.
mental_health_outcome: Adverse events from mental health apps, especially symptom deterioration, worsening mental health symptoms, hospitalization, self-harm/suicidal ideation, death, physical complaints, cognitive impairments, distress due to in-app features or technical difficulties, cyber sickness, financial concerns, relationship problems, and stigmatization fears.
positive_effects: The paper notes that growing evidence from randomized controlled trials shows mental health apps can effectively reduce a range of mental health symptoms and may be useful adjuncts in severe mental illness. In the adverse-event analyses, deterioration rates did not significantly differ between app and control groups (OR = 0.79, 95% CI = 0.62–1.01), suggesting no clear evidence that apps increased deterioration overall in the available data.
negative_effects: Only 55 of 171 clinical trials (32%) reported adverse events. Meta-analytic deterioration rate from 13 app conditions was 6.7% (95% CI = 4.3, 10.1; I2 = 75%). Severe adverse events reported across trials included hospitalization/re-hospitalization (14 trials), self-harm or suicidal ideation/intent (11 trials), death (3 trials), violent episode (1 trial), and crisis care referral (1 trial). Other adverse events included poorer overall mental health, subjective mood/anxiety/stress/psychotic symptom increase, physical complaints, financial concerns, relationship problems, increased stigmatization fears, cognitive impairments, distress due to technical difficulties, distress due to in-app features, feeling too reliant on the app, and cyber sickness. The introduction also cites concerns that chatbots may offer harmful advice and encourage destructive behaviors.
evidence_type: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials with quantitative meta-analysis of deterioration rates and qualitative synthesis of other adverse events.
main_finding: Adverse-event reporting in mental health app trials is inconsistent and limited. Only one in three trials reported adverse events, reporting methods were heterogeneous, and detail was often insufficient to judge app-related risks. The pooled deterioration rate in app conditions was 6.7%, and deterioration rates did not significantly differ from control groups. AI/chatbot-specific evidence was sparse and not the main focus of the review.
limitations_bias: Only a small number of trials reported deterioration data, so estimates are preliminary and may not represent all app trials. Definitions of deterioration varied across studies. Adverse events may be underestimated due to dropout and poor reporting of dropout reasons. The review included only randomized controlled trials and only the main outcome paper from each trial, so safety data from uncontrolled studies or supplementary/forthcoming publications may have been missed. Many trials did not clearly describe how adverse events were assessed. The review is largely about mental health apps broadly rather than AI-specific tools.
relevance_to_our_review: Indirectly relevant. This paper provides evidence on harms and adverse events associated with digital mental health apps, including limited mention of chatbot/AI-related risks. It is useful for contextualizing safety concerns around AI in mental health, especially possible harmful advice from chatbots and inadequate adverse-event monitoring, but it is not an AI-focused review and most included interventions were not AI-based.
notes_for_research_question: Use mainly for background on safety/harms of digital mental health interventions and for the statement that chatbots have at times offered harmful advice and encouraged destructive behaviors. Not ideal as core evidence for AI effects on mental health because the review aggregates mostly non-AI smartphone apps and reports only minimal chatbot-specific data.

title: A scoping review of large language models for generative tasks in mental health care
type_of_paper: Scoping review
population: Review of 16 included studies involving healthcare providers, patients, and the general public in mental health-related contexts; some studies included adolescents, students, psychiatric outpatients, and community participants.
ai_type_application: Large language models (LLMs) for generative mental health applications, including clinical assistance, counseling, therapy, emotional support, positive psychology interventions, and education. Frequently studied models were OpenAI GPT series (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT4-Turbo, customized GPTs), with some studies using PanGu, T5, and DialoGPT.
mental_health_outcome: Depression, anxiety, bipolar depression, ADHD, loneliness, stress, suicidality/self-harm, positive and negative affect, life satisfaction, psychological well-being, cognitive distortion/negative thoughts, social emotions, and abuse-related constructs.
positive_effects: The review reports initial promise of LLM-based mental health applications. Examples summarized by the authors include improvements in mental well-being, reductions in anxiety, increased life satisfaction in GPT-based positive psychology interventions; reduced emotional intensity and overcoming negative thoughts in cognitive restructuring interventions; enriched patient records and better insights for clinicians in journaling support; meaningful engagement with adolescents on mental health topics; reduced loneliness; and some self-reported cessation of suicidal ideation after chatbot interaction. LLMs also showed promise in simulated psychiatric decision support and generation of clinically relevant information.
negative_effects: Current evidence does not support use as standalone interventions. Major concerns include limited clinical validation, inconsistent and non-standardized evaluation methods, widespread use of ad-hoc scales, poor comparability across studies, under-evaluation of safety/privacy/fairness, lack of transparency and reproducibility due to reliance on proprietary models and web interfaces, limited reporting of demographics and target populations, possible bias and fairness issues, insufficient security/privacy evaluation, uncertain generalizability, and lack of long-term outcomes.
evidence_type: Systematic/scoping review of 16 studies identified from 726 unique records using PRISMA-informed search methods.
main_finding: LLMs show early promise for generative tasks in mental health care, but the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and methodologically weak. Evaluation has focused more on usefulness and engagement than on foundational issues such as safety, privacy, and fairness, and the available evidence is insufficient to justify LLMs as standalone mental health interventions.
limitations_bias: The review highlights substantial heterogeneity across studies; many use ad-hoc, non-validated scales; limited clinical validation; small or inconsistent sample sizes in many studies; inconsistent construct definitions; insufficient demographic reporting; lack of long-term follow-up; underassessment of safety, privacy, transparency, explainability, accountability, security, and resilience; dependence on proprietary closed-source models; some studies relied on website interfaces rather than controllable APIs; and reproducibility is limited.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a synthesis of evidence on AI effects on mental health from generative LLM applications. It summarizes both beneficial and concerning effects across multiple mental health outcomes, while emphasizing weaknesses in evidence quality and safety evaluation.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is useful as background and evidence mapping rather than as a direct effect estimate. It identifies candidate primary studies on AI/LLM effects on mental health outcomes and notes reported beneficial effects such as reduced anxiety, improved well-being, reduced loneliness, and reduced negative thought intensity, but also emphasizes that evidence remains preliminary and often lacks rigorous clinical validation.

title: The Application and Ethical Implication of Generative AI in Mental Health: Systematic Review
type_of_paper: Systematic review
population: Mental health service contexts globally; reviewed 79 peer-reviewed original studies published from October 1, 2019, to September 30, 2024. Included studies covered general population, vulnerable/underserved groups (eg, psychiatric outpatients, LGBTQ individuals, sexual harassment survivors, children with ADHD, older adults), clinicians, and mental health professionals.
ai_type_application: Generative AI, primarily large language models (LLMs) and GPT-based systems, used in three domains: (1) mental health diagnosis and assessment, (2) therapeutic tools such as chatbots/conversational agents, and (3) clinician support including decision support, documentation, therapy support, psychoeducation, training and simulation. Models mentioned include GPT-3/3.5/4/4o, ChatGPT, Gemini, PaLM 2, LLaMA, Mistral, Falcon, T5/Flan-T5, Alpaca, Wizard, and RAG/fine-tuned/hybrid variants.
mental_health_outcome: Depression, suicidality/suicide risk, anxiety, stress, emotion recognition/affective states, obsessive-compulsive disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, PTSD, ADHD-related mental health support, resilience, mindfulness, relationship distress, problematic smartphone use, preoperative anxiety, and general emotional support/well-being.
positive_effects: GenAI showed promise in augmenting mental health care by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, increasing accessibility to support, and reducing clinicians' administrative burden. In diagnosis/assessment, studies reported high precision for suicide risk prediction (up to 0.96) and promising depression detection performance (eg, 0.902 using semistructured diaries). Multimodal approaches improved reliability over text-only methods. As therapeutic tools, many studies reported positive user experiences such as affective relief, perceived empathy, self-reflection, and measurable benefits like reduced anxiety and reduced problematic smartphone use. For clinician support, GenAI showed usefulness for treatment planning, case formulation, prognosis assessment, summarization, cognitive restructuring support, psychoeducation, and training/simulation. Overall 17/20 therapeutic studies reported positive outcomes.
negative_effects: Ethical and safety concerns were consistently reported. Risks included privacy and data security concerns, bias and unfairness across demographic groups, reduced cross-cultural adaptability, hallucinated or inaccurate medical/mental health content, inconsistency across prompts/runs, poor crisis detection/management, emotional abandonment when conversations were terminated, overtrust by users, repetitive or generic responses, and insufficient safety mechanisms. Some models underestimated suicide risk, failed to flag explicit self-harm prompts, generated harmful substance-use advice, incorrect hotline information, nonexistent drugs, or inappropriate content. Real-world deployment and safety assurance were limited.
evidence_type: Evidence synthesis from 79 included peer-reviewed original studies identified via systematic review using PRISMA 2020. Reporting quality assessed with MI-CLAIM-GEN. The review provides narrative synthesis rather than meta-analysis due to heterogeneity.
main_finding: GenAI shows substantial promise across diagnosis/assessment, therapeutic support, and clinician support in mental health, but current evidence is largely early-stage, often based on proof-of-concept or simulated settings, with limited real-world deployment and major unresolved ethical, fairness, safety, and governance concerns. The authors propose the GenAI4MH ethical framework centered on data privacy and security, information integrity and fairness, user safety, and ethical governance and oversight.
limitations_bias: The review notes heterogeneity of study designs, datasets, and evaluation metrics, preventing quantitative synthesis/meta-analysis. Most included studies (70/79, 89%) focused on proof-of-concept or simulated interactions, with only 9/79 (11%) involving real-world deployment or longitudinal outcomes. Research was dominated by text-based language models. Social media datasets were common and may be demographically skewed toward younger, digitally active, predominantly English-speaking users, limiting generalizability and raising bias concerns. Reporting quality was moderate overall; reproducibility, harm assessment, representativeness of training data, and postdeployment evaluation were often underreported.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a recent systematic review directly synthesizing evidence on the effects of generative AI on mental health outcomes, including both beneficial effects and harms/ethical risks across diagnosis, intervention, and clinician support use cases.
notes_for_research_question: Useful umbrella source for mapping how AI affects mental health: includes positive effects such as improved detection, emotional support, anxiety reduction, behavioral improvement, and clinician efficiency, alongside negative effects including bias, hallucinations, privacy concerns, crisis-management failures, and overtrust. Because it is a review paper rather than a primary effects study, it is best used for background, citation chaining, and identifying primary studies on mental health outcomes.
